cim: If you write the code yourself, you’re going to win
cim_eredeti: If you write the code yourself, you’re going to win
szoveg_eredeti:
There’s been an outage where AI writes 50% of the code once again.

Yeah, yeah, blame it on something else. It isn't likely that a cyberattack brought JP Morgan down, that a latent bug that did the same to Outlook, or that excessive traffic (really!) brought put US airlines on the ground. Even the NSA was down, but they’re going to say it was a “scheduled routine maintenance”.

You don’t need to go full conspiratorial to link the widespread use of LLM generated code in production with the increased frequency of catastrophic software failures.

If you’re finally coming to terms with the explosive quality of using AI to do the writing, the coding, and the thinking for you, you’re not alone! But it’s hard to make sense of The New Way Of Doing Things when much of the economy is stagnant, and the only companies “thriving” (as per their share price) are the very ones telling you that AI is the future.

If you’re like me, you know that it is not sustainable to delegate the product you’re building to someone else—be it a machine or a human. You’ll build it with a higher quality, you’ll fix it faster when it breaks, and you’ll communicate what’s good for and for whom much more effectively if you build the product yourself.

It is tempting to put distance between you and the code that makes your product. Coding is, after all, mentally demanding, and we know from the work by Kahneman and Tversky that humans are repelled by mentally demanding work.

The promise of a machine that can do the low level thinking for us is too good to pass on.

Still, you must still write most of the code yourself. Not because LLMs don’t deliver; they may very well do. But because the writing of the code is the highest level of thinking you can make.

The reason I’m telling you all this is because nobody seems to agree with me. And that’s my unique advantage.

Now that everyone is letting the machine do their low-level thinking for them, I’ve realized that the impact of well thought, deliberately designed software is greater than ever. The problem has always been that we were in a rush and, never able to take the time to pay back the technical debt, didn’t remove the unnecessary bits and ended up producing undifferentiated software products.

We used to deliver good enough solutions to JIRA tickets that had to be completed against overly optimistic deadlines (often self-imposed).

However, if you build software that moves money around, you must admit to yourself that you’re not doing anything new: whatever piece of money software you’re building, someone else has already built it, often a decade before you. Not just similar stuff, but the exact same thing.

Which means that your task as an engineer isn’t really to build the thing, but to build an alternative that’s superior in a way that makes up for their decade-long head start.

In 2011, Kristo Käärmann and Taavet Hinrikus, two Estonian expats living in the UK, launched a company called Transferwise. They realized that, instead of going to a bank as individuals and exchange their kroons for pounds (with a 5% markup and a likely adverse exchange rate on top), they could swap their currency with each other, so that when one of them needed kroons and the other needed pounds, they could go around the need for banks. They called that “peer-to-peer currency exchange.”

In its first year of operation, transactions through Transferwise amounted to €10 million. The company became profitable in 6 years, and in 2021 it rebranded itself as Wise, going public with an 11 billion pound valuation.

And in 2024, the banking giant HSBC launched Zing, their own platform for currency exchange and international payments.

It was so blatant a copy, they even used Wise’s own brand colors (black and light green).

Mind you, we’re 13 years into Wise’s history, its product has been refined over and over, its customers are well understood, and a leaked internal memo from Santander UK admitted that the bank (or HSBC, for that matter) would lose 84 percent of its revenue if its charges were the same as Wise's.

13 years is a long time. Zing didn’t even lasted one.

Would Zing have had a chance if they had state-of-the-art AI models to work with back then?

It wasn’t speed of delivery what made Zing fail. It was the fact that, having a 13 year long head start, whoever was in need of what Zing had to offer was already a satisfied Wise customer.

The only way Zing would’ve been able to put up a fight against Wise is by building something different enough to attract unsatisfied Wise’s customers, or those who weren’t served well by Wise’s product. Not by creating an exact replica, and expect HSBC’s humongous size to do the rest.

Save the LinkedIn visionaries I remember reading when it launched, it was very obvious to everyone that Zing was going to be a flop. Which brings me, again, to the point of building money software with your own hands.

An LLM can only generate code that’s been trained on; it can never give you something remarkable. It is a human thing to look at the world and see what’s missing.

So, look at the world, see what’s not there and should. And start typing.

This was it for this week in The Payments Engineer Playbook. I’ll see you next week.

Feel free to share this article with a colleague.

P.S. I help fintech companies diagnose ledger problems before they become irreversible. If you feel that a second pair of eyes could be useful, check out how you can engage my services.
